doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

chapter: Roots in the church and Africa
title: The church, spirituals and the roots of the blues
summary: Roker traces blues singers, Parker and Gillespie back to the church and spirituals in the cotton fields, with slaves' drums taken away.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: You know I want to ask you something else you know, back to some aspects of church, particularly the African-American church. You know when I listen to preachers, they’re not necessarily singers, but I hear in their voice a certain cadence, you know, and it’s almost like it’s musical construction.
Yeah, they’re blues singers. That’s where blues singers come from man, listening to them deacons getting ready for the preacher.
Give us an example. Give us an example.

I’m not too good at it, [humms]—I can’t really do it. But I know it when I hear it. But everything comes out of the church. Well you know the spiritual value of music is something that you must have. Spirit. That’s what the blues comes from, see, the Gospel. And the Negro spirituals in the corn field. Because see they took the drums away from us when we were slaves because we could communicate with each other. And they wanted to separate us, the slave masters. And when we was working on the plantation. So we learned Gospel music. They would make up spiritual songs like [sings] lead me to the water. You know and they would send messages that way, see? And out of that come the blues singers like Dinah Washington and Sarah Vaughan. They come out of the churches, and Mahalia Jackson, you know, she was a spiritual singer, but if you listen to Aretha Franklin, you know what I’m saying? Ray Charles. See but and then it kept evolving.

Then you’ve got Charlie Parker, you’ve got Coleman Hawkins, they started swinging a little more and Ben Webster and Benny Carter, and it got more advanced with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. See but it all come out of the fields. See it come out of them cotton fields, you know, with the Negro spiritual. It’s real sophisticated now. You go in the church and they’ve got drums and everything, bass you know? I mean dreadlocks. The Baptist churches, you go and look on the pulpit there’s a set of drums up there with two tom toms all around and bass and it sounds to me just like James Brown and them.

You know now you were talking about the communication with the spirituals. Basically they would say if a man was working in a field next to a pretty woman and he was singing “Steal Away,” he wasn’t talking about God, he was talking about, hey if you were half as tired of working as I am after you get off tonight let’s hook up.
The beat goes on you know. Even God said, “go forth and multiply.” You know that’s very important. You know there’s always a way.
